PREFACE Lakṣmīdhara’s *Kṛtyakalpataru* is easily the most important [work of its kind].
It is also the earliest extant work and the most complete *nibandha* (digest) of *Dharmaśāstra* that has been handed down to us. Some of the earlier works of this class mentioned by it in...

The verses that introduced the entire work at the beginning of the *Brahmacārikāṇḍa* are now lost; like the famous *Smṛti* of Bṛhaspati, the citations from them that occasionally appear [in other texts] are likewise unavailable.

Later *nibandhas* such as the *Ratnākara* and the *Vīramitrodaya* were likely composed using secondary sources, as the original works had probably perished during the deluge of the Muslim conquest in the twelfth century.
The *Kalpataru* itself nearly shared this fate. The holy city of Kāśī, where it was likely composed, was repeatedly sacked;
the mounds near Rājghāt mark the buried remains of its ruins.
It was the most important part of the capital of Govindacandra. More than half of the work has survived in solitary manuscripts, which has made the task of editing it one of exceptional difficulty.

5.15 [The Blessed One said: "Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are four kinds of self-nature (svabhāva). What are the four? They are: the imagined self-nature (parikalpita-svabhāva), the dependent self-nature (paratantra-svabhāva), the perfected self-nature (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva), and the self-nature as the ultimate truth (paramārtha-svabhāva). Mahāmati asked: "What is the characteristic of the imagined self-nature? The Blessed One replied: "It is like the appearance of hair-tufts for those with cataracts, or like the forms of men, women, elephants, horses, cars, and foot-soldiers appearing in a dream; it is like the city of the Gandharvas, or like a mirage, a reflection, or an echo. It is the grasping at signs (nimitta) and names (nāman) based on objects that do not exist. This is called the characteristic of the imagined self-nature. Mahāmati asked: "What is the characteristic of the dependent self-nature? The Blessed One replied: "It is the manifestation of the mind (cittadṛśya) arising from the habit-energy (vāsanā) of false discrimination. It is the non-existence of external objects, yet it appears as if they exist due to the power of delusion. This is called the characteristic of the dependent self-nature. Mahāmati asked: "What is the characteristic of the perfected self-nature? The Blessed One replied: "It is the state where the dependent self-nature is seen as being eternally free from the characteristics of the imagined self-nature. It is the realization of the non-arising of all phenomena through the cessation of false discrimination. This is called the characteristic of the perfected self-nature. Mahāmati asked: "What is the characteristic of the self-nature as the ultimate truth? The Blessed One replied: "It is the realm of the Tathāgatas, which is beyond words, free from the duality of existence and non-existence, and realized by noble wisdom (prajñā). It is the state of being neither born nor destroyed, neither permanent nor impermanent, and is the essence of all Buddhas. This is called the characteristic of the self-nature as the ultimate truth. At that time, the Blessed One recited these verses:

"The imagined nature is like a hair-tuft for those with cataracts, Like a dream, a city of Gandharvas, a mirage, a reflection, or an echo. The dependent nature is the mind's own manifestation, Arising from the habit-energy of false discrimination. When the dependent is seen as free from the imagined, This is known as the perfected nature. The ultimate truth is the realm of the Tathāgatas, Beyond words, free from existence and non-existence, Neither born nor destroyed, neither permanent nor impermanent— This is the essence of all Buddhas. Thus spoke the Blessed One. Delighted, the venerable Mahāmati and the assembly of monks praised what the Buddha had taught. 5.15•

10.14. The Blessed One said this: “Monks, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? Here, monks, one person dwells having abandoned both internal and external clinging; he has cut off craving, severed the fetters, and through right penetration, he has made an end of suffering. This, monks, is called the first kind of person found existing in the world. Furthermore, monks, one person dwells having abandoned internal clinging, but not external; he has cut off craving, severed the fetters, and through right penetration, he has made an end of suffering. This, monks, is called the second kind of person found existing in the world. ● 264 The Blessed One said: “Monks, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? They are: the person who is like a heap of filth, the person who is like a jewel casket, the person who is like a blue lotus, and the person who is like a white lotus.

And what, monks, is the person who is like a heap of filth? Here, monks, a certain person is born into a noble family, one of high birth, with great wealth, abundant property, and vast possessions; yet he lives a life of misconduct in body, speech, and mind. This, monks, is called the person who is like a heap of filth. “And what, monks, is the person who is like a jewel casket? Here, monks, a certain person is born into a noble family, one of high birth, with great wealth, abundant property, and vast possessions; and he lives a life of good conduct in body, speech, and mind. This, monks, is called the person who is like a jewel casket. “And what, monks, is the person who is like a blue lotus? Here, monks, a certain person is born into a lowly family, one of humble birth, poor, with little wealth, meager property, and scant possessions; yet he lives a life of good conduct in body, speech, and mind. This, monks, is called the person who is like a blue lotus. “And what, monks, is the person who is like a white lotus? Here, monks, a certain person is born into a lowly family, one of humble birth, poor, with little wealth, meager property, and scant possessions; and he lives a life of good conduct in body, speech, and mind. Furthermore, he attains to the realization of the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, or the fruit of arhatship. This, monks, is called the person who is like a white lotus. These, monks, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world.”

265. The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, while practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, beheld that all five aggregates were empty and thereby delivered all suffering. Śāriputra, if there are any sons of good family or daughters of good family who wish to practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they should thus perceive all phenomena as empty in nature and should take refuge in the mind of enlightenment. Why is this? Because when one takes refuge in the mind of enlightenment, one transcends all worldly dusts and afflictions; one attains ultimate nirvāṇa, and because one has attained ultimate nirvāṇa, one is called a Tathāgata. Therefore, know, Śāriputra, that all the Buddhas of the three times, by relying on the *prajñāpāramitā*, have fully awakened to unsurpassed, complete, and perfect enlightenment. Therefore, know, Śāriputra, that the *prajñāpāramitā* is the great spiritual mantra, the great bright mantra, the unsurpassed mantra, the unequaled mantra, which pacifies all suffering and is true, not false. Thus, the mantra of the *prajñāpāramitā* should be spoken: Gate gate pāragate pārasaṃgate bodhi svāhā. Śāriputra, thus should the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā*. At that time, the Buddha repeated the mantra: Gate gate pāragate pārasaṃgate bodhi svāhā. When the Blessed One had finished speaking this sutra, the Venerable Śāriputra, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, the entire assembly of bhikṣus, and the world with its gods, humans, asuras, and gandharvas, having heard the Buddha’s teaching, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. This is presented in four parts: (1) the title (*nāma*), (2) the homage (*namaskāra*), (3) the promise to compose (*pratijñā*), and (4) the actual composition (*abhidhāna*). Regarding the title: "Guhyasamāja" means the assembly (*samāja*) of secrets (*guhya*). It refers to the gathering of the three secrets—the body, speech, and mind—of all Buddhas. Alternatively, it may be understood as the union (*samāja*) of the two secrets: the male and female deities. Furthermore, it signifies the integration of the two truths, the ultimate and the conventional, within the state of great bliss. Thus, it is called the *Guhyasamāja*. Regarding the homage: this consists of the homage paid by the author and the homage paid by the requester. As for the former, the author, the venerable master Nāgārjuna, pays homage to the Lord of Secrets (*Guhyapati*), who is the embodiment of the wisdom of all Buddhas, in order to generate faith in the practitioners. As for the latter, the requester, the bodhisattva Ārya-Mañjuśrī, pays homage to the same Lord of Secrets in order to inspire the listeners. Regarding the promise to compose: having paid homage, the author promises to compose the treatise in order to benefit sentient beings. He states that he will explain the meaning of this tantra, which is difficult to understand, by relying upon the instructions of his spiritual mentor. Regarding the actual composition: this is the exposition of the tantra itself. It is divided into two parts:

the introductory section (*nidāna*) and the main body (*śarīra*). The introductory section establishes the setting, the teacher, the audience, and the time. By this, he indicates that the practice of dharma is the means for attaining the highest goal. Furthermore, by using the term "always," he shows that one must practice dharma throughout all stages of life, from birth until death. He then explains the nature of dharma: "Dharma is what is taught in the Veda. This means that dharma consists of those actions prescribed in the Veda as conducive to the attainment of the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*). He further clarifies its source: "It is also found in the Smṛtis and in the conduct of virtuous men. Here, "Smṛti" refers to the works composed by the ancient sages based on the Veda; "conduct of virtuous men" refers to the behavior of those who are learned in the Vedas and free from passion; and "self-satisfaction" refers to the internal conviction of the mind regarding what is right. He concludes by stating that these four constitute the sources of dharma. Thus, having established the definition and sources of dharma, he now sets forth the specific duties of the various social classes and stages of life. First, he describes the general duties common to all: "Non-violence, truthfulness, refraining from theft, purity, and control of the senses—this is declared to be the general dharma for all. Among these, "non-violence" means not causing harm to living beings through thought, word, or deed; "truthfulness" means speaking only that which is beneficial and consistent with the truth; "refraining from theft" means not taking what belongs to another; "purity" refers to both external and internal cleanliness; and "control of the senses" means restraining the organs of perception and action from their respective objects. These are the duties common to all four castes and all four stages of life. Next, he describes the specific duties of the householder, who is the foundation of all: "To serve his mother and father, to perform his own sacred duties, and to attend upon the teacher—these are the primary duties of the householder. He then describes the duties of the student (*brahmacārin*): "One should study the Vedas under a teacher according to the rules, remaining chaste and subsisting on alms. He further specifies the duties of the forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*): "Having completed the stage of the householder, one should enter the forest, abandoning all possessions and maintaining the sacred fires. Finally, he describes the duties of the wandering ascetic (*parivrājaka*): "When he has renounced all attachments and is indifferent to the pairs of opposites, he should wander alone, seeking liberation. Thus, having established the general and specific duties, he concludes the section on the duties of the various orders. Now, he addresses the duties of the king, who is the protector of the world: "The king should protect his subjects according to dharma, punishing the wicked and honoring the virtuous. He further describes the king's personal conduct: "He should be proficient in the three branches of knowledge, self-controlled, and devoted to the welfare of his people. He then outlines the king's judicial duties: "In disputes between two parties, he should investigate the case according to the evidence and the law, and deliver a just verdict. Finally, he describes the king's religious duties: "He should perform sacrifices according to his capacity, give gifts, and protect the Brahmins. Thus, the duties of the king have been fully set forth. Now, he turns to the duties of the Vaiśya: "Agriculture, trade, animal husbandry, and the lending of money at interest—these are the duties of the Vaiśya. He then describes the duties of the Śūdra: "Service to the higher castes is the duty of the Śūdra; he should perform it with a pure heart. Having thus described the duties of the four castes, he now describes the duties of the four stages of life (*āśramas*). First, he describes the student: "A twice-born man, having been initiated, should dwell as a student in the house of his teacher, controlling his senses and studying the Vedas. He then describes the householder: "Having studied the Vedas and obtained the permission of his teacher, he should enter the state of the householder, marrying a wife of equal status. He further describes the forest-dweller: "When he perceives wrinkles, grey hair, and grandchildren, he should retire to the forest, abandoning all worldly ties. Finally, he describes the wandering ascetic: "When he has become detached from all things, he should renounce the world and wander as a mendicant, seeking the Self. Thus, the duties of the four stages of life have been described. Now, he describes the duties of the mixed castes (*saṃkara-jāti*): "From the intermixture of the castes arise various mixed castes, each with its own specific duties. He concludes by stating that one who performs his own duty according to his caste and stage of life attains the highest bliss: "By performing his own duty, even a lowly man attains perfection; by doing otherwise, even a noble man falls. Thus ends the exposition of the duties of the various castes and stages of life. Now, he describes the penances (*prāyaścitta*) for the expiation of sins: "For the removal of sin, one should perform penance according to the gravity of the offense, following the rules prescribed in the Veda. He further specifies the penances for the most heinous crimes: "For killing a Brahmin, drinking liquor, stealing gold, or violating the teacher's bed—one must perform the penance prescribed for each. He then describes the penances for minor offenses: "For other sins, one should perform penance according to the rules, whether through fasting, recitation, or charity. He concludes by stating that one who has performed the appropriate penance is purified: "Thus purified by penance, the soul becomes bright and fit for union with the Supreme. Thus ends the section on penances. Now, he describes the laws concerning inheritance and property: "Upon the death of the father, the sons shall divide the paternal estate equally, unless there be a special reason for inequality. He further describes the shares of the sons born of different wives: "Sons born of wives of the same caste shall take equal shares; those born of wives of lower castes shall receive a share less by one-quarter. He then describes the rights of the daughters: "If there are no sons, the daughters shall inherit the estate, provided they are unmarried or have not had children. He further describes the rights of the widow: "If there are no heirs, the widow may maintain herself from the estate, provided she remains chaste. He concludes by stating that property should be used for the benefit of the family: "Property should never be wasted; it should be used for the maintenance of the household and for acts of piety. Thus ends the section on inheritance and property. Now, he describes the laws concerning marriage: "Marriage should be contracted with a girl of equal caste and character, after due consideration of family and lineage. He further describes the eight forms of marriage: "Brahma, Daiva, Arsha, Prājāpatya, Āsura, Gāndharva, Rākṣasa, and Paiśāca—these are the eight forms of marriage. He then describes the duties of the husband and wife: "Husband and wife should live together in harmony, supporting each other and performing their religious duties. He further describes the grounds for divorce: "If the wife is barren, or bears only daughters, or is incurably diseased, or wastes the wealth—the husband may take another wife. He concludes by stating that the marriage bond is indissoluble: "The marriage rite is established by the giving away of the girl; once performed, it cannot be revoked. Thus ends the section on marriage. Now, he describes the laws concerning food and drink: "One should eat food that is pure and prepared with care, avoiding meat and intoxicants. He further describes the rules for guests: "A guest who arrives at mealtime should be honored with food and water, for he is a deity in human form. He then describes the rules for eating: "One should eat sitting on a clean seat, facing the east, and without criticizing the food. He concludes by stating that one who eats improperly incurs sin: "Eating while criticizing the food, or eating at improper times, leads to the loss of merit. Thus ends the section on food and drink. Now, he describes the laws concerning purification: "After voiding urine or excrement, one should cleanse oneself with earth and water according to the rules. He further describes the purification of various substances: "Gold is purified by fire, silver by water, copper by acid, and iron by rust. He then describes the purification of the body: "The body is purified by water, the mind by truth, the soul by knowledge, and the intellect by wisdom. He concludes by stating that purity is the root of dharma: "Purity is the foundation of dharma; therefore, one should always strive for purity. Thus ends the section on purification. BRAHMACĀRIKĀṆḌA OF THE KṚTYAKALPATARU: AN ESTIMATE OF THE VALUE OF THE ĀŚRAMA SYSTEM The *Brahmacārikāṇḍa* of the *Kṛtyakalpataru*, a digest of law attributed to Lakṣmīdhara, provides a systematic exposition of the duties and stages of life (*āśrama*) for a student of sacred knowledge. This section offers a comprehensive framework for understanding the value and significance of the ancient Indian system of the four stages of life—namely, the student (*brahmacarya*), the householder (*gārhasthya*), the forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*), and the renunciant (*saṃnyāsa*). The treatise begins by establishing the foundational importance of the student stage as the very root of the social and spiritual order. It emphasizes that the acquisition of Vedic learning through disciplined study under a qualified preceptor is the primary duty of the youth. The text delineates the specific rules of conduct, including the observance of celibacy, modesty, and the performance of daily rites such as bathing, fire-worship, and the recitation of mantras. Furthermore, it outlines the various types of studentship, distinguishing between those who remain lifelong students (*naiṣṭhika*) and those who prepare for the subsequent stage of householdership (*upakurvāṇa*). Beyond the individual discipline of the student, the *Brahmacārikāṇḍa* highlights the broader societal value of the *āśrama* system. It presents the stages of life not merely as personal milestones but as integral components of a harmonious social structure. By assigning distinct roles and responsibilities to each stage, the system ensures the continuity of tradition, the preservation of dharma, and the orderly progression of individuals from youth to maturity, and ultimately to spiritual liberation. The text underscores that the integrity of the entire community depends upon the faithful adherence to these prescribed duties by its members at every level. In conclusion, the *Brahmacārikāṇḍa* serves as a vital testament to the enduring relevance of the *āśrama* scheme. Through its detailed prescriptions and philosophical reflections, it demonstrates that this ancient model was designed to cultivate both worldly excellence and spiritual realization, thereby maintaining the balance between material prosperity and ultimate transcendence. Its value lies in its ability to provide a coherent ethical and pedagogical framework that remains instructive for understanding the historical evolution of Indian civilization.

16.13. The Blessed One said this: “Monks, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? The person who is like a lotus flower growing in a pond; the person who is like a blue lotus flower growing in a pond; the person who is like a white lotus flower growing in a pond; and the person who is like a fragrant water lily growing in a pond. And how, monks, is a person like a lotus flower growing in a pond? Here, monks, a certain person dwells with his mind overcome by sensual lust, burning with sensual lust, unable to abandon that sensual lust. He sees another person dwelling with his mind overcome by sensual lust, burning with sensual lust, unable to abandon that sensual lust, and he envies him. He thinks: ‘How fortunate it is for me that I have not yet been reborn in such a state! It is in this way, monks, that a person is like a lotus flower growing in a pond. And how, monks, is a person like a blue lotus flower growing in a pond? Here, monks, a certain person dwells with his mind overcome by ill will, burning with ill will, unable to abandon that ill will. He sees another person dwelling with his mind overcome by ill will, burning with ill will, unable to abandon that ill will, and he envies him. He thinks: ‘How fortunate it is for me that I have not yet been reborn in such a state! It is in this way, monks, that a person is like a blue lotus flower growing in a pond. And how, monks, is a person like a white lotus flower growing in a pond? Here, monks, a certain person dwells with his mind overcome by sloth and torpor, burning with sloth and torpor, unable to abandon that sloth and torpor. He sees another person dwelling with his mind overcome by sloth and torpor, burning with sloth and torpor, unable to abandon that sloth and torpor, and he envies him. He thinks: ‘How fortunate it is for me that I have not yet been reborn in such a state! It is in this way, monks, that a person is like a white lotus flower growing in a pond. And how, monks, is a person like a fragrant water lily growing in a pond?

Here, monks, a certain person dwells with his mind overcome by doubt, burning with doubt, unable to abandon that doubt. He sees another person dwelling with his mind overcome by doubt, burning with doubt, unable to abandon that doubt, and he envies him. He thinks: ‘How fortunate it is for me that I have not yet been reborn in such a state! It is in this way, monks, that a person is like a fragrant water lily growing in a pond. These, monks, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world.”

101 13 The Blessed One said: “Ānanda, this is the first great miracle of the Tathāgata, which has not been seen by other śramaṇas, brahmins, devas, Māras, Brahmās, or by anyone in the world. “Furthermore, Ānanda, when the Tathāgata wishes, he emits from his upper body a stream of fire that blazes upward, while from his lower body he emits a stream of water that flows downward. Just as a skilled potter or his apprentice, using a well-prepared lump of clay, can produce whatever vessel they desire, so too, Ānanda, when the Tathāgata wishes, he emits from his upper body a stream of fire that blazes upward, while from his lower body he emits a stream of water that flows downward. This, Ānanda, is the second great miracle of the Tathāgata, which has not been seen by other śramaṇas, brahmins, devas, Māras, Brahmās, or by anyone in the world. “Furthermore, Ānanda, when the Tathāgata wishes, he makes his body invisible; yet those standing nearby think, ‘We see the Blessed One,’ though they do not see him. Then, having made himself visible again, those who were previously unable to see him now think, ‘We see the Blessed One. This, Ānanda, is the third great miracle of the Tathāgata, which has not been seen by other śramaṇas, brahmins, devas, Māras, Brahmās, or by anyone in the world. “Furthermore, Ānanda, when the Tathāgata wishes, he enters into the meditative absorption of the cessation of perception and feeling (saññā-vedayita-nirodha-samāpatti). Having emerged from that absorption, he reflects: ‘I have dwelt in the meditative absorption of the cessation of perception and feeling for one day, or for two days, or for three, four, five, six, or seven days. This, Ānanda, is the fourth great miracle of the Tathāgata, which has not been seen by other śramaṇas, brahmins, devas, Māras, Brahmās, or by anyone in the world. “Furthermore, Ānanda, when the Tathāgata wishes, he exercises mastery over the lifespan-karma (āyu-saṃkhāra) that was acquired in a previous birth. He thinks: ‘Let me maintain this lifespan-karma for a full century, or even longer. And he maintains it accordingly. Understand that dharma which is approved by the heart.

"By the learned" means by those who know the meaning of the Vedas. "Practiced" means constantly performed. "By the good" means by the virtuous. "Always" means that which is irreproachable and foremost.

By her [it is meant]: "by those free from hatred and passion" means by those who are devoid of attachment and aversion as inferred from scriptural injunctions; "approved in the heart" means accepted as something to be performed without hesitation. Viśvāmitra.
That which the noble ones who know the scriptures praise while it is being performed is Dharma;
that which they censure, they declare to be Adharma.

By "by the learned" (*vidvadbhiḥ*), those who know the meaning of the Vedas are meant; by "by the virtuous" (*sadbhiḥ*), valid cognizers (*pramātṛ*) are meant. Through these two qualifiers, the fact of being established by Vedic authority (*vedapramāpitatva*) is indicated. By "by those free from hatred and passion" (*adveṣarāgibhi�*), those devoid of attachment and aversion toward prohibited results are meant. Through this, the quality of not being productive of a powerful undesirable consequence (*balavadaniṣṭāprayojakatva*) is indicated.

By the phrase "approved by the heart" (*hṛdayenābhyanujñāta*), the quality of being a means to the highest good (*śreyassādhanatva*) is indicated; for it is precisely in such a case that the mind becomes oriented toward it.
Thus, the meaning is this: its essence (tattva) consists in being established by the Veda as a means to the highest good (śreyas), while not being prompted by a powerful desire for something else.

33. The Bodhisattva’s Great Compassion and the Ten Powers of a Tathāgata. Furthermore, Mañjuśrī, the bodhisattva mahāsattva, having cultivated the great compassion of a bodhisattva, attains the ten powers of a tathāgata. What are these ten? First, the power of knowing the difference between the faculties of beings; second, the power of knowing the inclinations and dispositions of beings; third, the power of knowing the various elements of beings; fourth, the power of knowing the paths leading everywhere; fifth, the power of knowing the recollection of former abodes; sixth, the power of knowing death and rebirth; seventh, the power of knowing the exhaustion of outflows; eighth, the power of the knowledge of the destruction of all afflictions; ninth, the power of the knowledge of the non-arising of phenomena; tenth, the power of the knowledge of the cessation of all conditioned things. Mañjuśrī, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva has perfected these ten powers of a tathāgata, he is called a “Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha. Why is this? Because, Mañjuśrī, the Tathāgata, having fully awakened to all phenomena as they truly are, possesses unimpeded wisdom and vision regarding all things. Therefore, he is called a “Tathāgata. Furthermore, Mañjuśrī, because the Tathāgata has abandoned all afflictions and their latent tendencies, and because his mind is liberated through perfect knowledge, he is called an “Arhat. Because he has realized the reality of all phenomena and taught them to others exactly as he has realized them, he is called a “Samyaksaṃbuddha. Thus, Mañjuśrī, it is by means of these ten powers that a bodhisattva mahāsattva becomes a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha. This is called the bodhisattva’s practice of the perfection of power. [page 138] Furthermore, Mañjuśrī, the bodhisattva mahāsattva, having cultivated the great compassion of a bodhisattva, attains the four fearlessnesses of a tathāgata. What are these four? First, the fearlessness of having attained supreme perfect enlightenment; second, the fearlessness of having exhausted all outflows; third, the fearlessness of having correctly explained the obstacles to the path; fourth, the fearlessness of having correctly explained the path to liberation. Mañjuśrī, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva has perfected these four fearlessnesses, he is called a “Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha. Why is this? Because, Mañjuśrī, the Tathāgata, having fully awakened to all phenomena as they truly are, is fearless in the midst of the great assembly and teaches the Dharma with confidence. Therefore, he is called a “Tathāgata. Furthermore, Mañjuśrī, because the Tathāgata has abandoned all afflictions and their latent tendencies, and because his mind is liberated through perfect knowledge, he is called an “Arhat. Because he has realized the reality of all phenomena and taught them to others exactly as he has realized them, he is called a “Samyaksaṃbuddha. Thus, Mañjuśrī, it is by means of these four fearlessnesses that a bodhisattva mahāsattva becomes a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha. 40. “O King, that which is called ‘the self’ is merely a conventional designation; it does not exist as a substantial entity. Just as the term ‘chariot’ is applied to a collection of parts, so too is the term ‘self’ applied to the aggregates. [page 155] “Furthermore, O Great King, the self is like a dream; it is empty, devoid of intrinsic nature, and lacks any real existence. It is like an illusion, produced by the power of conceptual construction, appearing through the force of habitual tendencies. [page 156] “Moreover, O Great King, the self is like a reflection; it arises dependent upon various conditions and has no independent essence. It is like an echo, produced by sound, lacking any permanent substance. [page 157] “In this way, O Great King, the self is a mere conceptual construct, arising from ignorance and craving. It is not found when sought through wisdom; it is like a mirage in the heat of the sun. [page 158] “Therefore, O Great King, one should abandon attachment to the self and cultivate the perception of non-self. By seeing all phenomena as empty and selfless, one shall attain liberation from the cycle of birth and death. [page 159] “Thus, O Great King, the self is a false notion, a fabrication of the mind. It is like a phantom created by a magician, appearing to exist while being utterly void of reality. [page 160] “Hence, O Great King, you should practice with diligence to realize the truth of emptiness. By understanding that the self is merely a name, you shall transcend all suffering. [page 161] “Furthermore, O Great King, the self is like a bubble on water; it arises and perishes in an instant. It is like a flash of lightning, appearing for a moment and then vanishing. It is like a cloud in the sky, formless and insubstantial. [page 162] “In short, O Great King, the self is a deceptive appearance, a product of delusion. It has no beginning and no end; it is neither born nor does it perish. To see it thus is to see the Dharma. [page 163] “Therefore, O Great King, do not cling to the notion of a self. Abandoning all views of a personal identity, you shall abide in peace, free from all afflictions. [page 164] “Thus, O Great King, the teaching of the non-existence of the self is the gateway to the noble path. By following this teaching, one shall reach the city of Nirvana, where there is no more birth or death. [page 165] “This is the true nature of things: that the self is ultimately unfindable. To understand this is to be liberated from the bonds of existence. [page 166] “Therefore, O Great King, you should always maintain mindfulness of the non-self. And this is the explanation by Caṇḍeśvara (*Kṛtyaratnākara*, 37): "Without a subject" means without scope in any particular matter. "By the purpose of the *Smṛti*" means by the purpose of the *Dharmaśāstra*; [it supersedes] the "purpose of the *Arthaśāstra*," such as the science of government (*daṇḍanīti*). Between two *Arthaśāstras* themselves, that which is based on logic (*nyāyamūla*) is authoritative. Regarding "for the sake of the unseen (*adṛṣṭārthe*)"—that is, regarding the purpose of the *Dharmaśāstra*—there is an option (*vikalpa*), provided that a consistent application (*vyavasthā*) is possible.

When the possibility of establishing a distinction does not exist, but it does exist [in another case], there is indeed a fixed rule (*vyavasthā*). Regarding the "option (*vikalpa*) between Smṛti scriptures," when there is a contradiction between two Dharmaśāstras, there is an "option. Regarding "the fulfillment of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣāpūraṇe*)," when there is an expectancy, in the case of its supplementation, there is indeed "combination" (*samuccaya*). By this, because they possess expectancy, the combination of Smṛti and the other sources is indicated.

2] The Blessed One said: “Ānanda, this is the Dharma-discourse called ‘The Great Compassion. It was taught by me in the past when I was a bodhisattva, and it has been practiced by all the Tathāgatas. Ānanda, if there are sons or daughters of good family who hear this Dharma-discourse of the Great Compassion, write it down, memorize it, recite it, explain it to others, and practice it according to the teaching, they will all attain supreme, perfect enlightenment. Furthermore, Ānanda, if there are those who, having heard this Dharma-discourse of the Great Compassion, feel even a single thought of joy, they will all be born in the presence of the Buddhas in the ten directions. If there are those who, having heard this Dharma-discourse of the Great Compassion, feel even a single thought of faith, they will all be freed from the three evil realms and never again fall into them. If there are those who, having heard this Dharma-discourse of the Great Compassion, feel even a single thought of reverence, they will all be protected by the gods of the four great kings and the devas of Trāyastriṃśa. If there are those who, having heard this Dharma-discourse of the Great Compassion, feel even a single thought of respect, they will all be able to see the Buddhas of the present in the ten directions and hear their teachings. Ānanda, if there are those who, having heard this Dharma-discourse of the Great Compassion, maintain it in their hearts without forgetting, they will all be able to fulfill the six perfections and quickly attain buddhahood. Therefore, Ānanda, you should know that this Dharma-discourse of the Great Compassion is the most supreme among all dharmas, the most profound, and the most difficult to encounter. You should always protect and uphold it. At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses: “The Great Compassion Dharma-discourse, Is the treasury of all the Buddhas. If one hears, writes, or recites it, One shall quickly attain enlightenment. It can deliver beings from suffering, And cause them to dwell in peace and bliss. It is the path for all bodhisattvas, Leading them to the city of Nirvāṇa. If one respects and reveres it with faith, One shall be born in the presence of the Buddhas. It destroys the three evil realms, And never allows one to fall back. The four great kings and the devas Will always protect such a person.

One shall see the Buddhas of the ten directions, And hear the Dharma without end. Maintaining this in mind without forgetfulness, One fulfills the six pāramitās. This is the supreme dharma, Profound and difficult to encounter. Therefore, you should always uphold it, To benefit all sentient beings. When the Buddha had spoken these verses, the Venerable Ānanda and the great assembly, hearing what the Buddha had taught, rejoiced and faithfully practiced it.

He who knows how to address someone should say, "I am so-and-so, sir. And he who does not...

One should know: when addressed in a salutation, the final vowel of that name receives the *bhobhāva* (the change to *bho*), as well as the status of a *saṃdhyakṣara* (diphthong) and the status of being *apragṛhya*, just as in the case of "bho bhāva."

"Whoever should know how to return a greeting"—the meaning is that when a greeting has been performed, one should perform a return greeting. One should greet such a person by mentioning their own name as a specific qualification. However, regarding one toward whom one does not know how to return a greeting...
The meaning is that one should say, "It is I here, sir" (*ayamaham bho*). By the word "and" (*ca*), women are also included.
And so Manu says [2.123]:
"Those who do not know how to perform the salutation by name..."

It should be made three morae (trimātra). "Diphthong" (saṃdhyakṣara) refers to *e*-kāra and so forth. "Non-pragṛhya" means devoid of the designation *pragṛhya*. Regarding the phrase “but one who has set out on a journey,” the meaning here is that even one on a staircase or the like may sit down. “If he does not sit down” means if he—his...

He should not proceed to announce the acceptance of the sacrifice. "Not seated behind" means he is not seated with his feet positioned differently from those of the other [students]. "Anuvāti" implies "when the wind is blowing";
"vītaḥ" means one whose face is turned away; that is, when the wind is blowing toward the teacher in that direction.

The meaning is that he should not stand. "Unsteady" (*apratiṣṭhabdhaḥ*) means not having made a support with his hand on the ground or elsewhere. "Not leaning on anything else" (*anapāśrito’nyatra*) means not resting his back or sides against something other than a wall or similar structure. "Wearing the sacrificial thread" (*yajñopavītī*) refers to one who has two garments; [the word] *yajñopavītī* [is used here]...

One should place a cloth over [the left shoulder]. "With the lower garment tucked up" (*adhonivīta*) means not covered by a portion of the lower garment. The syntactical connection is: "one should sit for as long as one can reach with both arms while seated. "Not employing the practice of sitting" (*anāsanayoga-vihita*) means without performing the formal preparation of a seat.

The grammatical connection is: "he should not sit. When the teacher is active—that is, performing an action—"he should desire to act" within the scope of the teacher's power, that is, in what is possible for him.
"Anvaksthāninam" means one who is not inferior to the teacher. "By lineage," and not by name.

‘Enam’ refers to the one standing behind. ‘Api cettasya guruḥ syāt’ means even if he were the teacher of that *brahmacārin*. In the phrase ‘nāmnā tadantevāsinam’, the connection is with ‘na kīrtayet’. ‘Nāmnā’ means by name—that is, by the venerable name. ‘Yasmiṃ—’ [The sentence continues: “In whom...”
"However, in the case of that best of the twice-born, there is respect and proper conduct toward one who is not his teacher [only] because of a connection with a teacher;
whereas in the case of one who is 'not a teacher'— that is, without a connection to a teacher— he is highly learned due to having acquired knowledge."
In the Kṛtyakalpataru,
[chapter] 12.
Because he is superior to one's own son and because of the performance of his duties, "respect" is well-known in the world;
the meaning is that "service"—that is, attendance—should be rendered toward him, who stands in the place of the teacher, just as it is toward the teacher. And having eaten of his...
Thus, having eaten in the presence of the teacher, one should not offer the leftovers without rising;

for it is prescribed that "one should present [the remains] to the teacher," meaning that the student in the stage of celibacy (brahmacārī) must offer what remains after he has eaten to the teacher, and this must not be done without rising.

‘He should not turn his back’ means that, desiring to go on business, he should not depart showing his back; rather, ‘having circumambulated [them] from the right,’ he should depart. Gautama [2.29–37]:

One should mention the name and lineage of the teacher with respect; likewise when honoring or toward one who is superior. One should respond [to a command] while rising from one's bed, seat, or standing place. One should approach [the teacher] when not seen by him, at his bidding. [One should remain] below him, on a lower seat, or in a position away from the wind.

Upon seeing his teacher, he should rise; he should follow him when he departs; having informed him of and reported upon his activities; he should study when summoned; and he should be intent on what is pleasing and beneficial [to the teacher].
‘Samānataḥ’ means having bowed properly. ‘Śreyān’ means superior by virtue of knowledge and other qualities. If he is honored in the world, then [one should behave] toward the teacher as...

All that has been mentioned, such as salutation and so forth, is to be performed by extension through the word [of the rule]. "Staying" means remaining; "leaving that" means having moved forward some distance.
"Responding" here refers to accepting the teacher's command. "Approaching" is from the verbal root *vac*.

"Upon seeing," "upon not seeing," or "from the guru"—that is, from the issuing of a command—there should be "approaching," meaning going toward him; the word "duty" (*kāryam*) is to be supplied as the object.
"Service regarding crosswinds" refers to the voiding of urine and feces, according to Kapardin. "One should rise."
From that place, he should go to another location. Having informed and declared the ritual action (*karma*), [he says]:
"This ritual action must be performed by the disciple for the teacher; I shall perform it."
12] In the section on the life of a religious student (brahmacārikāṇḍa), [chapter on] following the guru and teacher, verse 215.

The meaning is that one should remain after having informed, acted, and explained. "Yuktaḥ" means diligent; the word "should be" (syāt) is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence. "Pleasant" (priyam) refers to that which produces immediate pleasure;
"beneficial" (hitam) refers to that which produces happiness in the long run.
"Whether constantly urged by his teacher or even without being urged,
he should apply himself to study and to the welfare of his teacher."
Restraining his body, speech, organs of perception, and mind,
he should stand with palms joined in reverence, gazing at the face of the teacher.
He should always have his hand ready for service, be of virtuous conduct, and well-restrained;
and when told, "Be seated," he should sit down facing the teacher.
One should not engage in conversation or give a promise while lying down,
nor while sitting, nor while eating, nor while standing, nor with one's face turned away.
One standing should attend to one who is seated; one approaching should attend to one who is standing;
one going forward should attend to one who is coming toward him; and one running should attend to one who is running behind.
Facing one who has turned away, approaching the presence of one who is far off,
bowing to one who is lying down, and standing at the command of one who is seated.
In the presence of his teacher, his bed and seat must always be low;
within the teacher's range of vision, he should not sit as he pleases.
One should not utter his name alone, even in his absence;
nor should one imitate his gait, speech, or gestures.
Wherever censure or slander of the guru arises,
one should either cover one's ears or depart from that place to another.
Having read "yatnam" in the phrase "adhyayane yatnam," Kullūka has explained it as "udyogam" (or) "yogam."
The reading "yogam" is that held by Medhātithi; it is explained as meaning "effort" (yatnam).
2. "Susaṃvṛtaḥ" (well-restrained) is the reading held by Medhātithi.
In the Kṛtyakalpataru:
"One who utters slander becomes a dog; indeed, a reviler becomes a dog."

"Parivāda" is the public proclamation of faults; the other is "nindā" (censure). [The phrase] "from parivāda" means from causing [the censure] to be heard, because that is subject to censure due to its being prohibited. Medhātithi maintains that this prohibition mentioned previously is an *arthavāda* (an explanatory or declamatory statement).
One who consumes [the offerings] becomes a worm; one who is envious becomes an insect.
One should not salute him while standing at a distance, nor when angry, nor in the presence of a woman; likewise, if one is seated in a vehicle or on a seat, one should descend before saluting him.
One should not sit with one's teacher either to the windward or to the leeward;
nor should one say anything at all that cannot be heard by the teacher.
Likewise:
[2.218] Just as a man digging with a spade obtains water,
so does one who desires to listen obtain knowledge residing in the teacher.
"In a place out of earshot" (*asaṃśrave*) means a place where that which is being spoken is not clearly heard;
Bhaviṣya Purāṇa 6.
"O King, one should not disclose anything regarding the teacher's conduct;
'āvṛṇvṛtti' means that which conceals a secret. — Śaṅkha and Likhita.
He should not perform those things he has learned, except for matters of proper conduct;
nor should he address others with the discourses of the Vasiṣṭhas.
"Trained" means learned from the presence of the teacher; even those things not explicitly told by the teacher, such as his movements, speech, and gestures, were understood by him on his own.
This prior prohibition is an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*), according to Medhātithi.
12] Following the Guru and the Teacher, in the Section on the Student Life (Brahmacārikāṇḍa)

One should not engage in this [behavior] toward one's guru: "One should not converse with stories of the Vasiṣṭhas. This means that one should not speak in the presence of the guru with stories or praises concerning matters not instructed by the gurus.
Hārīta:
One whose vital energy is drawn upward (an *ūrdhvaretas*), while observing the vows prescribed by the Guru, [should perform] service to the Guru.

"One should act thus. Now, by fetching water-jars, *kuśa* grass, flowers, sacrificial fuel, roots, and fruits, and by performing sweeping, smearing [the floor], personal service, and so forth, one should follow him with devotion whether he is walking, standing, or lying down. Always doing everything for him, observing vows, one should not [discard] his remains from offerings.
One should not step over a bed, a seat, a shadow, or wooden sandals.

"Ūrdhvaretas" means one who has restrained the emission of semen. "Aṅgaśuśrūṣā" refers to the act of massaging the limbs. "Sarvakārī" means one who performs all that is appropriate. Thus says Paiṭhīnasi.
One should please the teacher with tooth-sticks, bedding, seats, coverlets, massage, kind words, and so forth.
Āpastamba [1.2.19–20]:
He should remain dependent on his teacher, except in cases involving acts that cause loss of caste; he should act for the benefit of his guru and not oppose him with his speech.
Śaṅkha says:
"Without contradicting [the teacher] with speech," meaning one should not speak words that are contrary to the teacher.
Neither by bathing, nor by burnt offerings, nor even by the service of the sacred fire does a celibate student go to heaven; he goes there through the worship of his teacher.
Free from egoism, one should perform what is beneficial and pleasing for the guru with devotion.
Yama in the Kṛtyakalpataru, verse 218.
[12] One must never depart without having first taken leave of one's teacher;
furthermore, whatever task is to be performed by a disciple or even by a servant, [it should be done with his permission].
While living with his teacher, the student should be intent upon the duties of the guru;
he should always be devoted to darbha grass and fuel, dedicated to the fire-rituals, and remain pure.
With palms joined in reverence, he should say to the teacher: "O Blessed One, I shall study.
[The phrase] "or as a servant" implies that even the work of a servant must be performed by the student.
This follows from the continued application of the word "he should avoid."
Gautama [2.20–21]: In the presence of one's teacher, one must avoid covering the neck, sitting with the knees bound together, leaning against a support, stretching out the feet,
spitting, laughing, yawning, and cracking the knuckles.
"Kaṇṭhaprāvṛtam" means covering the neck. "Avasakthikā" is the binding of the hands above the knees. "Avasphoṭanam" is the cracking of limbs such as the fingers. Viṣṇu [32, 10–12]:
One should not engage in contentious debate with the teacher, nor should one speak ill of him, nor anything that is disagreeable to him.
‘Vigṛhyakathā’ is a debate for the sake of victory.
Nārada—[p. 142, verse 8]:
“Until he has mastered the sciences, the disciple should remain diligent in his service.”
1. The reference in S. B. E., Vol. II, p. 187 is different, namely II, 14–15, [pp. 334–334].
12] In the section on the life of a religious student (brahmacārikāṇḍa), [chapter] 219: Following the Guru and the Teacher.
Āpastamba [1.4.22–28]:

He should also avoid sleep. Furthermore, day by day he should protect his teacher through actions consistent with dharma and artha. Having protected him, when going to bed, he should say: "Protect dharma."

"Do not be ashamed of me. If the teacher should, through negligence or intentionally, violate a rule, the student should point it out to him in private. If he does not desist, the student should either undertake the duties himself or cause him to desist.
Furthermore, one who rises before [the teacher] and goes to bed after him...
They say of him, "He does not sleep. For one who has thus directed his self as a student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacārin*),
all his actions here become fruitful and attained,
even those which pertain to the life of a householder.

"One should avoid sleep"—the ellipsis is "one should protect [it] both before and after. This is because of the injunction that follows: "Now, as for him who rises early and goes to bed late, they say of him, 'He does not sleep. [The phrase] "joined with dharma and artha" means "conducive to dharma."

"By means of fetching sacrificial fuel, flowers, *kuśa* grass, and so forth—things useful for ritual purposes—as well as by bringing food and the like; 'protect the Dharma, do not let it perish,' [the form] *mā jūgupamah* is used with the particle *māṅ* in the *luṅ* (aorist) tense. Therefore, this is the meaning: 'In this way I protect the Teacher, and now may the Dharma protect me.'"
"Transgression of the rules" refers to such acts as failing to honor guests and so forth. Paiṭhīnasi states:
"One who possesses fortitude and gains wealth should report it to his teacher, except for praise."
One should announce: "This has been done; this will be done. Baudhāyana says:
"For these [students] should speak the truth, be free from pride, rise before [their teacher], and go to bed after him."
He is one who abides [in truth], whose words as a guru are everywhere unimpeded, except in the case of a transgression.
In the presence of his teacher, he should always have inferior food, clothing, and attire. *In the Kṛtyakalpataru:* [He should be so].
"Even for one who has returned home from his teacher, this same set of customary rules (*sāmāyācārika*) applies regarding these [matters]. Just as..."

The conduct of a religious student (*brahmacārin*): He should not wear garlands, nor have his face smeared, nor have his hair and beard anointed, nor be dyed, nor smeared with unguents; he should not wear turbans, head-wraps, tunics, sandals, or wooden shoes. He should neither perform nor cause others to perform these things during formal rituals, nor during private activities.

Just as with the cleaning, massaging, and scraping of the teeth, the teacher should not speak of those substances when they are in contact with himself. However, some say that a *snātaka*, when invited or approached at the proper time according to the rule, should not refuse what has been brought to him. [He should not speak] more loudly...

He should not sit upon anything with many legs, nor upon anything supported on all sides. He should not occupy a bed or seat already used by another. If traveling by vehicle, he should mount it after his teacher; likewise, he should mount carriages, palanquins, and poorly spread beds only after his teacher. He should not address his teacher unless he is first addressed himself, nor should he speak to him with merely pleasant words.

Furthermore, one should avoid poking at the teacher, whispering to him, laughing at him, addressing him familiarly, calling him by his personal name, or sending him on errands. One may inform him of matters concerning one's welfare only when there is an emergency.
While living with him, one should go to see the teacher every morning and evening unless summoned.

And having returned from a journey, he should see [the teacher] on that very day. In the event of a meeting between the teacher and the sub-teacher (prācārya), he should first clasp the feet of the sub-teacher and then desire to clasp the feet of the teacher. The other (the sub-teacher) should forbid him.
In the presence of the teacher, his [the sub-teacher's] honor is eclipsed; however, he may visit the teacher’s family from time to time for the purpose of seeing them.
One should go according to one's ability, even taking with one an elephant-tusk used for cleaning the teeth.

The meaning is this: "Just as the *vṛtta*—that is, the conduct or performance—of a student (*brahmacārin*) who has returned home [is prescribed], so too is this very same *sāmayācārika* [conduct] for one who has returned home. For one who has "returned home" (*samāvṛttasya*), that is, one who lives together [with his wife] prior to marriage by virtue of necessity.
‘Mālī’ means one who wears garlands; ‘āliptamukhaḥ’ means one whose face is smeared all over with sandalwood paste.
In the section on the student's life (brahmacārikāṇḍa), [this concerns] obedience to the guru and the teacher.

221. *Dāliptamukhaḥ*: "One whose hair and beard are smeared. Here, the prefix *upa-* has the sense of "properly"; thus, it refers to one whose hair and beard have been properly prepared by means of shaving and so forth.

‘Anointed’ (aktaḥ) means one who has applied collyrium to the eyes; ‘rubbed with oil’ (abhyaktaḥ) means one who has performed an oil massage. ‘Veṣṭitī’ means one who wears a turban; ‘upaveṣṭitī’ means one who has wrapped a cloth around the waist.
‘Kañcukī’ means one who wears a bodice; ‘upānahī’ and ‘pādukī’ refer to one who wears sandals or shoes.

This is well known. Regarding "in noble conducts" (*udācāreṣu*), that is, when acts such as embracing and so forth are being performed toward a teacher or the like of superior character, one should not perform these [acts] such as touching (*mālita*) and so on;
nor should one cause them to be done by another, nor upon oneself. As for the word "and" (*ca*):
Regarding the meaning of the word, he states an exception to [the rules on] being a garland-maker (*mālī*) and so forth: "And in voluntary acts" (*svairi-karmasu*).
With respect to one's own affairs, one should neither perform nor cause these acts of being a garland-maker and so forth to be performed. He describes what constitutes voluntary acts: "As follows..."
By the words "the channels," and so forth; "combing" refers to the grooming of the hair with a comb (*kaṅkatika*) or similar tools.
In this context, he states the duty of the teacher by way of an incidental discussion:
"of those materials," meaning the clothing and other articles belonging to the resident pupil; "by means of personal contact," meaning by [the teacher's own] self—

"Connection" (*saṃyoga*) here refers to the relationship between master and servant; for that reason, he "should not speak"—he should not engage in conversation. The meaning is that one who is "smeared" (with worldly attachments) should not speak of his virtues.
Furthermore, he states the duties of one who has returned [from studentship] with the words beginning, "But the *snātaka* at the proper time," and so forth.
At the time of the return ceremony (*samāvartana*), that which was brought according to the rules and accepted with mantras—

such as the umbrella, garland, ointment, earrings, and so forth— is called "brought" (*abhihṛta*). Then, having been summoned by the teacher or having gone toward the teacher himself, he should not withdraw his own body [from the service].
Regarding this, some teachers say: "In a place with many feet," meaning in a non-monastic community and so forth;
[and] "the cleaning of the teeth."
The mention of the "mouth" is an elliptical indication (upalakṣaṇa), according to the statement of Āśvalāyana [Gṛhyasūtra 3.7.10]: "A Brāhmaṇa should smear [the ointment] on his face and limbs."

The teacher, having gone to the pupil's house, should not speak in such a way that his desire for gain is perceived—for instance, by saying, "Oh, what a beautiful vessel for food! and so forth. [This is because of the mention of] "some" [in the rule]. However, according to the view of our own school (Āpastamba), he should even abandon that [desire for gain] himself.
Haradatta:
In the Kṛtyakalpataru.

Regarding the term *adhyācarite*, it means "having been used. As for the phrase "one who is joined to a vehicle should follow on the road," it means that when told by the teacher, "Mount the vehicle," one should mount it later on the road.
The grammatical connection is: "One should ascend the *sabhānikaṣa* with the teacher. *Sabhā* is a place for a gathering of people.
*Kaṭaḥ* is a wooden plank or similar object used for leveling a field of loose earth. *Vyupeta-doṣaḥ* means [one who is] free from various faults such as [improper] finger-movements and so forth.
*Taudana* refers to [the act of] eating boiled rice. *Vyupajāpa* means various whisperings in one's vicinity or into the ear.
*Vyabhihāsa* means joking in the presence of a superior. *Udāmantraṇa* means calling out loudly.

One should call out to a teacher who is nearby and not deaf with a loud voice. Regarding "mentioning by name," the mention of the name given by the father and others is forbidden, but not that of other venerable names, as such is seen in the conduct of the learned. "In times of distress, one should make oneself known" means "in distress," that is, when suffering from pain.

*Artha* means purpose. One should inform the teacher of one's effort by another means. Regarding the phrase "on that very day," the mention of "day" is for the sake of illustration; one should go at that very time even if it is night. *Upasaṃjighṛkṣet* means one should manifest the desire to perform the formal salutation (*upasaṃgrahaṇa*).

"He should perform [the salutation] by extending his hands and so forth. "The other" refers to the teacher (ācārya). "Of him" means of the teacher. Regarding the phrase "he should go for the purpose of seeing [him]," this refers specifically to one who has returned home from study (samāvṛtta), as established by the context. "Adhihastya" refers to roots, fruits, and so forth, which are found in the hand.
The meaning is that he should go while holding [the teacher] by the hand himself.
Regarding service to the teacher, Śaṅkha and Likhita state:
"One should not stand alone on a seat or a bed, except at a sacrificial altar, in a palanquin," and so forth.
From vehicles, carts, followers, and those present at auspicious occasions:
"Followers" refers to those who have followed a corpse; "those present at auspicious occasions" refers to those assisting at weddings and the like, standing as officiating priests (*adhvaryu*).
1. *Svastara* means a bed of *palāśa* leaves; [this is] Haradatta’s [explanation].
2. *Vyupajāpa* means the repeated whispering in the ears; [this is] Haradatta’s [explanation], [Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa] 1.8.22.
12] On following the Guru and the Ācārya, in the Section on the Life of the Religious Student (Brahmacārikāṇḍa)
On vehicles drawn by cattle, horses, or camels, on couches, on terraces, and on mats;
One should sit together with the teacher even upon stone slabs, wooden benches, or boats.
Baudhāyana states: "There is no fault in sitting together on a boat, a stone slab, a wooden plank, an elephant, a palace, a rampart, or on anything provided with wheels."
Regarding wheeled vehicles such as carts and the like:
Āpastamba [1.7.20–23].
If the teacher is in distress, he may obtain [the required wealth] from an Ugra or even from a Śūdra.

Some say that it is always lawful to obtain the teacher’s requirements from a Śūdra or an Ugra. Having given [something], he should not speak of it; and having performed [a service], he should not call it to mind.
Hārīta says: "One who has fallen into difficulty" means one who has met with calamity.
Indeed, the teacher [should uplift] that disciple who is smeared with the mire of ignorance and struck down by darkness.
It quickly washes away [impurities] with the water of the knowledge of conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra).
Whether one receives a verse, a half-verse, a quarter-verse,
or even a single syllable from the presence [of a teacher], there is certainly great reverence due to that [teacher].
Even a guru, if he is arrogant, ignorant of what ought and ought not to be done,
and has set out upon a wrong path, is ordained to be abandoned.
He who neither teaches nor studies, but conducts himself according to the whims of others— a teacher endowed with such characteristics must be abandoned by the student observing his vows.
But the disciple who treats with contempt a teacher who has acted rightly takes upon himself the teacher's misdeeds and goes to a birth among the animals.
In the *Kṛtyakalpataru* (The Wish-Fulfilling Tree of Duties) [page 339].
Āpastamba [1.14.2–4]:
One should not reject him on account of his study or on account of a command. Not...
And one should not perceive any fault in this; for when there is no restraint, destiny alone prevails in that case.
He who covers both ears with his actions that are not false—
He should be known as one's mother and father; one should never bear ill will toward him.
Viṣṇu [30.43]: From whomever one receives knowledge— whether it be worldly, Vedic, or even spiritual— one should never cause that person harm.
Vasiṣṭha: [2.10–11] He who covers the ears with that which is not false— hearing what is free from suffering and bestowing immortality— [is a true teacher].
One should consider him as both father and mother,
for he has not withheld anything from him.
Those Brahmins who, having been instructed, do not respect their teacher in word, thought, or deed—
they indeed are not worthy of being fed by the teacher.
In that very same way, that sacred learning does not benefit them.

1. If, by "chance" (*yadṛcchayā*), that is, without a visible cause such as intellectual deficiency and so forth, the state of study were not accomplished; and if the portion studied did not reach another student, then in that case, service to the teacher (*ācārya-śuśrūṣā*) alone would be the recourse. (Haradatta)
2. "By Brahmā" is the reading recorded by Medhātithi and Kullūka;
3. "Or even" is the reading recorded by Nandapaṇḍita.
12] In the section on the student life (brahmacārikāṇḍa): obedience to the guru and teacher,
and likewise their extension [to others].
Regarding this, Viṣṇu states:
[32, 1–2] A king, a sacrificial priest, a learned śrotriya, one who prohibits unrighteousness, a teacher, and a paternal uncle—...
My maternal grandfather, maternal uncle, father-in-law, teacher, elder brother, and paternal relatives are to be honored like a preceptor (ācārya). So too are their wives of the same caste (savarṇā).
When the teacher’s own teacher is present, one should behave toward him as toward one's own teacher;
and unless permitted by one's teacher, one should not pay homage to one's own teachers.

But for the teacher of knowledge, this alone is the constant mode of conduct: toward those who forbid unrighteousness and even those who impart what is beneficial, one should behave exactly as toward one's own elders.
One should always behave toward those who are superior exactly as one does toward the guru—
toward the guru’s sons, toward those worthy of respect, and toward the guru’s own kinsmen.

‘Of the guru’ means of the one who initiates and imparts the Veda. ‘Like the guru’ means in that very same manner. ‘Unreleased’ means not commanded. ‘His own’ refers to the guru’s sons and others. ‘The teacher of knowledge’ (vidyā-guru) means the sub-teacher (upādhyāya). ‘Constant’ means pertaining to all times. ‘In his own kin’ (svayoniṣu) [refers to those related by blood].

Regarding paternal uncles and others: "among those who are superior" means those enriched by learning and austerity; "among teachers" refers to those belonging to the three higher castes. Āpastamba [1.14.5–9]:

One should serve one's mother, father, and teacher as [one would serve] a preceptor. Upon returning from a journey, all elders should be saluted by clasping their feet; likewise upon reunion after living abroad. Among brothers and sisters, the same salutation is performed according to seniority. And worship should be performed daily, in accordance with the instructions.
‘According to seniority’ means according to the order of age. ‘According to instruction’ means in the manner previously stated, such as “the left [hand] with the left,” and so forth.
In the *Kṛtyakalpataru* (The Wish-Fulfilling Tree of Duties).
Again, Āpastamba [1.13.12–18]:
[12] "There is no going outside the sacrificial ground (*bahirvedi*). [One should not go to] one who is teaching what has been assigned [to him for study]..."

One should undertake the recitation of the Veda. Some say that one should always [address the teacher] as "Arhat. There is no [fixed] rule regarding this. However, among the elders, when there is a mutual application of the term "Brahman," there is no fixed rule;

Regarding the phrase "not outside": because that which is outside the Veda, such as the scriptures of the Buddhists and others, is an *apayāna* (a path of departure), no *gati* (destiny) exists for it. 11.3.0.11 Non-study periods (anadhyāya):

Thunderbolts, earthquakes, and the appearance of Rāhu or meteors are immediate [impediments]. So too are thunder, rain, and lightning when fires have been kindled during the day outside the rainy season; and at night, from the latter part of the night until the third watch.
When these occur for even a third of the night, all [the study] is suspended. A meteor is equal to lightning.

According to some, [the impurity lasts] until the thunder ceases; during the afternoon; or even at nightfall. For the entire night until midnight, and for the day as long as there is light, [there is impurity]. Also when the king residing in one’s territory has died, and when one has traveled abroad and returns together with another. [Impurity also occurs upon] a commotion, a fire, the completion of a Veda-study, or vomiting.

One should observe a fast for a day and a night after partaking in a *śrāddha*, a human sacrifice (*manuṣyayajña*), or a feast; likewise on the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*). Or, one may observe it for two days. This applies to the full moon days of Kārttika, Phālguna, and Āṣāḍha. One should observe it for three nights during the three *aṣṭakā* festivals; some say only during the last one. One should observe it for the period surrounding the rainy season (*vārṣika*). All [these rules apply] when there is rain, lightning, or thunder.

In the case of a *saṃnipāta* caused by exertion, it lasts for three nights; likewise in a *saṃnipāta* involving discharge. After a meal, during a festival, and after beginning one's Vedic study, [the impurity lasts] for four *muhūrtas* at night.
Some say it is constant in a city. Even mental [impurity makes one] impure. For those performing a *śrāddha*, it lasts until the same time the next day.
And also when there is contact with one who has not performed a śrāddha for the deceased; and those [impurities] which they prescribe for each specific branch of knowledge (vidyā).
The term "day" (*ahaḥ*) is an elliptical expression for a period of four *praharas*. Regarding "during the rainy season" (*ṛtau*), it means during the rains;

when clouds and rain are seen at the time the sacred fires have been kindled, there is a suspension of study for the day. By this, it is indicated that the "immediate suspension" (*ākālikatva*) mentioned immediately prior applies to occasions other than the rainy season. Regarding "lightning" (*vidyuti*):
In the *Kṛtyakalpataru* [18]:
"During the rainy season, when [the moon] is visible at the time of the evening twilight, there is no study at night. That...

Beginning from the third part of the afternoon, when lightning occurs at the time of the evening or morning twilight and continues until the end of the day or the afternoon, there is no study during the night; and by the word "and" (*ca*), it is understood that there is also no study during the day or the afternoon when lightning occurs at the time of the morning twilight, continuing until the end of the latter part of the night.

It is thus stated that it is "to the limit. Regarding the phrase "starting from a third part," Jayasvāmin explains that when lightning flashes persisting from the third part of the night or day up until the evening and morning twilights, there is no study at all during that entire night or until the end of that entire day.
Regarding the term "ulka" (meteor): according to the opinion of some, there is no study during a meteor, just as there is none during lightning.

"Stanayitnu" refers to thunder; this, occurring in the afternoon, constitutes a period of non-study equal to that of lightning. "Api pradoṣe" means that even at nightfall, if thunder occurs, it is likewise [a time for non-study].

He performs the non-study (manadhyāya) [rule]: "If it is day" (ahaścit)—if a cloud persists before the afternoon, then there is non-study until the end of the day. "In whose territory" (viṣayasthe)—when the king of the country where the student resides has died, there is non-study, but not otherwise.

"In the country" refers to the rule "and having traveled abroad," because the suspension of study for the duration of the absence of the pupil or the teacher was previously introduced. The mention of the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite prior to the [mention of] the feet (the *pārvaṇa*) is for the purpose of indicating specific faults, similar to how specific penances (*prāyaścitta*) are prescribed for the annual rites (*ābdika*) and others; it refers to those occasions. Since non-study [of the Veda] would already have been established by this rule, the repetition is for the purpose of stating an excess of fault. Regarding "the three Aṣṭakās," these are those following the Āgrahāyaṇī full moon.
Regarding "one on the last," some hold that there is a three-night period of non-study on the last Aṣṭakā. For those who hold [this view]—

The *aṣṭikā-karman* is performed on the eighth day (*aṣṭakā*) of that [lunar month]; this refers to that specific occasion. "In *prasyandin*" means other than during the rainy season. [Page 408] The Blessed One said: “Ānanda, when a noble disciple possesses four qualities, he is one who has entered the stream, is no longer subject to rebirth in the lower realms, and is firmly established for full enlightenment. What are these four? Here, Ānanda, a noble disciple possesses unwavering confidence in the Buddha: ‘The Blessed One is an arahant, perfectly enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One. He possesses unwavering confidence in the Dhamma: ‘The Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One, directly visible, immediate, inviting one to come and see, applicable, to be personally realized by the wise. He possesses unwavering confidence in the Saṅgha: ‘The Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing the good way, practicing the straight way, practicing the true way, practicing the proper way; that is, the four pairs of persons, the eight types of individuals—this is the Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples, worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, the unsurpassed field of merit for the world. And he possesses the virtues dear to the noble ones—untorn, unbroken, unblemished, unmottled, freeing, praised by the wise, ungrasped, leading to concentration. “Ānanda, when a noble disciple possesses these four qualities, he is one who has entered the stream, is no longer subject to rebirth in the lower realms, and is firmly established for full enlightenment. [End of page 408]

Provide your translation in English: "Furthermore, O son of noble family, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive the perfection of generosity as a real entity, nor does he perceive the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditation, or the perfection of wisdom as a real entity.

He does not perceive form as a real entity, nor does he perceive feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as a real entity. He does not perceive the eye as a real entity, nor does he perceive the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as a real entity. He does not perceive forms as real entities, nor does he perceive sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena as real entities. He does not perceive the eye-consciousness as a real entity, nor does he perceive the ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, or mind-consciousness as real entities. He does not perceive the contact of the eye as a real entity, nor does he perceive the contact of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as a real entity. He does not perceive the feeling born of the contact of the eye as a real entity, nor does he perceive the feeling born of the contact of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as a real entity. He does not perceive the earth element as a real entity, nor does he perceive the water element, fire element, wind element, space element, or consciousness element as a real entity. He does not perceive the door of liberation of emptiness as a real entity, nor does he perceive the door of liberation of signlessness or the door of liberation of wishlessness as a real entity. He does not perceive the fruit of stream-entry as a real entity, nor does he perceive the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, or arhatship as a real entity. He does not perceive the fruit of pratyekabuddhahood as a real entity, nor does he perceive the state of a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha as a real entity. Why is that? Because all these dharmas are empty of intrinsic nature; they are ungraspable and cannot be apprehended. Since they are empty of intrinsic nature, they do not exist, and because they do not exist, they are not apprehended. This is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s practice of the perfection of wisdom."
